extracted.intended_audience: USPTO policymakers, patent examiners, patent practitioners, and other stakeholders in U.S. patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: A formal USPTO study evaluating alternative restriction standards and implementation options for U.S. patent examination, including four specific reform options, their operational procedures, and projected impacts on quality, workload, pendency, and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current statutory/MPEP restriction standard (35 U.S.C. §121; MPEP §803)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may properly be required to be restricted to one of two or more claimed inventions only if: (1) they are able to support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct; and (2) search and examination of the entire application involves a serious burden (MPEP §803).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Office's baseline practice intended to balance granting reasonable breadth of protection in a single patent against the burden on the USPTO of examining multiple inventions in a single application. Implementation involves identifying separate inventions, grouping claims, stating reasons, and requiring an election to prevent abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT Unity of Invention (PCT Rule 13) (as a candidate standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT Rule 13.1: 'The international application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a general inventive concept.' Under Option 2 the unity concept is applied so that multiple inventions constitute a single inventive concept if there is a technical relationship among the claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding 'special technical features.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under USPTO-modified Option 2, any purported special technical/common feature must also comply with 35 U.S.C. §112, first paragraph (in addition to novelty and non-obviousness). Where necessary in large applications, the applicant will be invited to identify a reference claim to facilitate determining 'same or corresponding' features. If no response to an invitation to pay additional fees, current PCT practice searches the first mentioned invention; the study notes public preference for allowing applicants to choose a 'main' invention and for abandonment (not defaulting to the first mentioned) if no response is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 1: Current practice with option to pay for additional inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the current 35 U.S.C. §121 'independent or distinct' standard, but allow applicants to request and pay for examination of up to 2 additional independent or distinct inventions, and to request and pay for examination of up to 10 species (per invention) at an additional per-species cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process essentially mirrors current restriction practice: identify separate inventions, group claims, briefly describe each claimed invention, state reasons relied upon, provide option to pay before examination, permit payment under protest (fees may be partially/fully reimbursed if protest justified). This option is expected to be least disruptive and require the least additional examiner training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 2: Modified PCT unity of invention with pay option and reference-claim procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a modified PCT 'unity of invention' standard nationally, with the additional requirement that any purported special technical/common feature comply with 35 U.S.C. §112, first paragraph, and allow applicants the option to pay for concurrent examination of up to two additional inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applications contain a large number of inventions (e.g., chemical/biotech), applicant will be invited to identify a reference claim. The first claimed invention is searched (as in PCT practice) to provide a reference point. If applicant does not respond to restriction/election, abandonment under current practice will apply. Implementation requires more training than Option 1 but less than Options 3 or 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 3: Three-tier fee structure (substantially similar / related / unrelated)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard based on whether inventions are 'related or unrelated' with fees determined by a three-tiered structure: tier 1 ('substantially similar') pays a base fee; tier 2 ('related') requires an additional fee/surcharge for inventions that raise substantially different patentability issues but do not require a substantially different search; tier 3 ('unrelated') comprises inventions that require additional searching and present dissimilar patentability issues and would not be permitted to be examined in the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally, examiner first identifies inventions using current independent-or-distinct grouping; applicant must elect a reference invention and may request/payment for placement of remaining inventions into tiers. If placement into tiers is requested and paid for, the Office issues a second communication with the placement and invitation to pay for up to 4 additional inventions in tier 2. No option is provided to pay for tier 3 inventions to be examined within the same application (tier 3 inventions would require divisional filings). The study found Option 3 complex to implement and train on, requiring multiple communications and decisions, and therefore decreased predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 4: 'Independent and distinct' reinterpretation of 35 U.S.C. §121
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-interpret §121 to require inventions subject to restriction be both 'independent and distinct.' Distinct means patentable over each other; independent means there is no common feature(s), or there is a common feature(s) but the common feature(s) does not define over the prior art and/or satisfy the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. §112 (first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In initial restriction requirements where independent inventions share a common feature(s), the examiner should infer that the common feature(s) fails to define over the prior art (an inference that may be rebutted). Applicant may 'provisionally elect' an invention and define common feature(s) (or may identify them on filing); otherwise the examiner will identify the common feature(s) and applicant may rebut. Examiner searches elected invention; if elected invention is patentable, examiner continues a 'rolling' search of the common feature(s) (or nonelected inventions that require it) until either an unpatentable related invention/common feature is found or all are found patentable. An additional fee is required for restriction/election where at least one common feature exists. The study found Option 4 to be the most difficult to understand and implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core aims/metrics for restriction reform (public-comment goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments proposed a number of goals for restriction reforms: increase cost-effectiveness; promote quality patents; enhance predictability of restrictions; encourage the examination of all claims to the same invention or inventive concept by the same examiner; encourage filing of fewer divisional applications; and promote harmonization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These goals were used to evaluate candidate standards and to shape study questions; trade-offs among these goals (e.g., cost-effectiveness vs. examiner workload) are central to selecting an option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation complexity, training, and monitoring as an evaluation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any change to the restriction standard and business processes requires initial training and continued monitoring of all personnel to assure proper and consistent implementation; the extent of training depends on the significance of changes from current practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewers' feedback survey measured perceived difficulty to train and achieve consistent implementation; implementation difficulty increases across Options 1→2→3→4. The TC 1600 Action Plan includes measures (published training, second pair-of-eyes reviews, published examples) to mitigate quality issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on output, pendency, and revenue as evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how each option affects examiner production (output), application pendency, number of divisional/RCE/continuation filings, and USPTO revenue; analyses referenced FY2006 budget assumptions and modeled examiner staffing and revenue implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key assumptions included that allowing more concurrent examination would reduce divisional filings (assumed 50% reduction for modeling), but also increase per-application examiner time (reducing per-examiner throughput), and possibly increase RCE/continuation filings. Any transition likely requires revised fee structure to maintain revenue. Effects on output/pendency/revenue were compared against FY06 baseline estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study sampling and reviewer methodology standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Study sampling methodology: target sample size 475 applications over a one-year period, target error rate 4.5–5 percentage points at 95% confidence; stratification and post-weighting across Technology Centers; monitor unavailable selections for bias; independent second review of 15% of applications; reviewers were patent-examining managers with subject expertise; regular meetings to assure consistent interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precautions to control non-sampling error included expert reviewers, periodic calibration meetings, feedback surveys to gauge reviewer opinions, and independent re-reviews to monitor variability. These standards are used to assess the reliability of the business-case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: TC1600 Restriction Practice Action Plan (quality-improvement criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 5-point action plan for Technology Center 1600 to improve restriction quality and consistency: (1) publish examples of claim sets; (2) emphasize rejoinder practice (include form paragraph reminding applicants of rejoinder); (3) deliver and publish updated examiner training targeted to workgroups; (4) implement enhanced second pair-of-eyes review for restrictions (first and subsequent actions); (5) continuous assessment via sampling, monitoring second restrictions, and customer surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational steps are intended to reduce improper restriction requirements, improve predictability, and provide training materials publicly. Implementation priorities include focusing on high-impact art units first and immediately starting form paragraph and second-pair-of-eyes initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback survey evaluation dimensions and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers rated the four Options on expected ease/difficulty across tasks using a 10-point scale (1 = most easy, 10 = most difficult), with current 35 U.S.C. §121 standard set at '3' for comparison. Tasks rated included: (a) ability to understand and apply the criteria to groups; (b) ability to understand and apply the criteria to species; (c) opinion on training of Examiners to apply criteria to groups; (d) opinion on training of Examiners to apply criteria to species; (e) preparing a restriction requirement; (f) expected overall consistent implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric results reported: Option 1 ~3.5, Option 2 ~5.1, Option 3 ~6.4, Option 4 ~7.9 for a representative task; the survey quantifies perceived implementation difficulty and was used to inform recommendations (Options 1 and 2 preferred over 3 and 4).
